title: Suicide Risk: Immediate Safety Beats Privacy
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: A patient expressing suicidal intent, a plan, access to lethal means, or inability to remain safe requires immediate protection and escalation. Do not leave a high-risk patient alone while arranging the next level of care.
recognize: Specific plan, intent, recent attempt, escalating hopelessness, command hallucinations, intoxication, agitation, or access to lethal means increases urgency.
priorities: Stay with the patient or ensure continuous observation per policy and remove accessible hazards when safe.
Notify the RN/provider/emergency mental-health pathway immediately.
assessMonitor: Use direct questions about thoughts, plan, intent, means, recent behavior, substance use, and protective factors within role/policy.
interventions: Maintain a safe environment and follow ordered observation/transfer precautions.
medicationSafety: Medication administration does not replace suicide precautions; monitor for overdose access and activation/agitation when clinically relevant.
redFlags: Cannot commit to immediate safety plan
teaching: Emergency help is appropriate when suicidal thoughts become active or safety cannot be maintained.
delegationScope: Observation may be assigned to trained staff, but suicide-risk interpretation and escalation require licensed clinical oversight.
examTrap: Leaving the patient alone to obtain paperwork because they promised not to act.
oneLinePearl: Active suicide risk is a safety emergency, not a confidentiality exercise.

title: Escalating Violence: Safety, Space, and Help First
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Escalating threats, weapon access, severe agitation, or loss of behavioral control require immediate staff/patient safety measures and team escalation. Do not corner, challenge, or physically confront the patient alone.
recognize: Pacing, clenched fists, escalating volume, threats, fixation, intoxication, paranoia, and weapon-seeking are danger cues.
priorities: Maintain personal space and an exit route, reduce stimulation, summon trained assistance, and move bystanders when possible.
assessMonitor: Monitor behavior, triggers, intoxication/medical contributors, response to de-escalation, and environmental hazards.
interventions: Use calm, simple communication and clear behavioral limits; follow emergency/security procedures when danger escalates.
medicationSafety: Emergency medication/restraint use requires orders/protocols and monitoring; never use medication as punishment or staff convenience.
teaching: When stable, review triggers and safer coping/help-seeking strategies.
delegationScope: Only trained personnel should participate in physical intervention; PN/LVN authority varies by state/facility.
examTrap: Standing between an agitated patient and the door while arguing about rules.
oneLinePearl: Do not win the argument—win safety.

title: Panic Attack: Reduce Stimuli and Rule Out Medical Danger
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Severe anxiety can cause chest tightness, dyspnea, dizziness, and fear of dying, but first-time or atypical cardiopulmonary symptoms still require medical evaluation. Once immediate medical danger is addressed, use calm presence and simple directions.
recognize: Hyperventilation, trembling, palpitations, paresthesias, intense fear, and inability to process complex information are common during panic.
priorities: Assess ABCs/vital signs and concerning medical features, then reduce stimulation and stay with the patient.
assessMonitor: Monitor symptom onset, chest pain characteristics, oxygenation/vitals as indicated, triggers, substance use, and response to support.
interventions: Use short statements, slow breathing coaching without forced paper-bag rebreathing, and grounding.
medicationSafety: Administer ordered anxiolytics cautiously and monitor sedation/respiratory effects; avoid assuming medication is the only intervention.
teaching: After recovery, identify early cues and coping strategies and follow the treatment plan.
delegationScope: Vital signs may be delegated; interpretation of atypical symptoms and escalation require licensed judgment.
examTrap: Labeling first-time crushing chest pain as anxiety before assessing medical danger.
oneLinePearl: Panic can mimic emergencies; emergencies can also look like panic.

title: Trauma-Informed Care: Ask, Explain, Offer Choice
bottomLine: Trauma-informed care reduces avoidable re-traumatization by emphasizing safety, transparency, collaboration, and choice. Explain what will happen before touching or exposing the patient whenever the situation allows.
recognize: Startle, freezing, dissociation, hypervigilance, avoidance, or distress during procedures may reflect trauma responses.
priorities: Create physical/emotional safety and ask permission before nonemergency contact when possible.
assessMonitor: Observe distress, triggers, communication preferences, support-person needs, and ability to participate.
interventions: Offer choices that do not compromise care, narrate procedures, protect privacy, and stop when safe if distress escalates.
medicationSafety: Sedation should not be used merely to overcome understandable trauma-related distress without appropriate indication.
teaching: Patients can state preferences and request explanations/support within the limits of urgent care.
delegationScope: All staff can use trauma-informed communication; clinical risk assessment remains with licensed clinicians.
examTrap: Forcing a nonurgent procedure without explanation because cooperation is expected.
oneLinePearl: Safety includes how care is delivered.

title: Intimate Partner Violence: Private Screening and Safety Planning
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: When abuse is suspected, create privacy, use nonjudgmental direct questions, assess immediate danger, and connect the patient with appropriate resources. Do not confront the suspected abuser or promise reporting rules that vary by jurisdiction.
recognize: Injuries inconsistent with explanation, controlling partner behavior, repeated visits, fearfulness, strangulation history, threats, or reproductive coercion raise concern.
priorities: Interview privately when safe and assess immediate danger, strangulation, weapon threats, children/dependents, and safe disposition.
assessMonitor: Document objective findings and patient statements according to policy.
interventions: Offer advocacy/social-work resources and individualized safety planning; follow applicable reporting law.
medicationSafety: Consider whether a controlling person is withholding, misusing, or monitoring medications when planning safe care.
teaching: Leaving can increase danger for some patients; safety planning should be individualized rather than directive.
delegationScope: Screening/reporting duties vary by role, state, age, and circumstance; follow law and facility policy.
examTrap: Telling the patient to leave immediately without assessing whether that increases danger.

title: Elder Abuse: Injury, Neglect, and Exploitation Need Escalation
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: Unexplained injuries, neglect, medication withholding, financial exploitation, fearfulness, or caregiver intimidation require private assessment and reporting/escalation according to state law and facility policy.
recognize: Patterned bruising, pressure injuries from neglect, malnutrition, poor hygiene, missing medications, sudden financial changes, or caregiver control are cues.
priorities: Address urgent medical needs, create privacy when safe, and notify the designated safeguarding/reporting pathway.
assessMonitor: Document objective findings, functional/cognitive status, statements, caregiver behavior, and immediate safety.
interventions: Engage social work/adult protective resources as required and plan a safe disposition.
medicationSafety: Missing, duplicated, or intentionally withheld medication can be a form of neglect/exploitation and requires reconciliation.
teaching: Provide accessible information on help resources when safe to do so.
delegationScope: Mandatory-reporting requirements vary by jurisdiction and setting; follow state law and facility policy.
examTrap: Accepting a caregiver's explanation without privately assessing the patient when abuse cues are present.
oneLinePearl: Protect, document objectively, and follow the reporting pathway.

title: Acute Grief: Support Without Pathologizing Normal Loss
bottomLine: Grief varies widely. Listen, support cultural/spiritual preferences, assess function and safety, and avoid treating expected grief reactions as automatically pathological.
recognize: Sadness, yearning, sleep/appetite changes, crying, anger, guilt, and fluctuating functioning may occur after loss.
priorities: Assess safety, coping supports, basic needs, and whether symptoms are causing severe or persistent impairment.
assessMonitor: Monitor suicidal thoughts, substance use, inability to perform basic care, psychosis, and prolonged severe impairment.
interventions: Use presence, open-ended questions, practical support, and referral when risk or persistent dysfunction is present.
medicationSafety: Sedatives/alcohol can worsen falls, respiratory risk, and coping; medication should not be used simply to suppress normal grief.
teaching: There is no single correct timeline for grief; seek help when safety or daily function deteriorates.
delegationScope: Supportive presence can be shared across the team; risk assessment/escalation require licensed oversight.
examTrap: Telling the patient they should be moving on by a certain date.
oneLinePearl: Grief needs support; danger and severe dysfunction need escalation.

title: Agitated Older Adult: Delirium Until Medical Causes Are Considered
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: New agitation, hallucinations, or confusion in an older adult can reflect delirium from infection, hypoxia, medication toxicity, pain, retention, dehydration, or metabolic illness. Do not assume a psychiatric cause or chronic dementia.
recognize: Acute onset, fluctuating attention, altered level of consciousness, sleep-wake reversal, and abrupt functional change favor delirium.
priorities: Assess physiologic causes and immediate safety while notifying the RN/provider.
assessMonitor: Trend vitals, oxygenation, glucose as indicated, pain, urine/stool retention, medication changes, hydration, and infection cues.
interventions: Use orientation, glasses/hearing aids, sleep support, mobility, hydration, and calm environment while treating the cause.
medicationSafety: Sedatives and anticholinergic drugs can worsen delirium; review recent medication changes.
teaching: Families should report abrupt changes from baseline.
delegationScope: Behavior observations may be delegated; interpretation of acute change requires licensed assessment/escalation.
examTrap: Requesting a sedative before checking for hypoxia, infection, pain, or retention.
oneLinePearl: New confusion is medical until proven otherwise.

title: Behavioral Restraint: Last Resort, Not Convenience
